subject: Chemistry
topic: Functional groups in organic chemistry — mixed tiers
description: OH, COOH, CHO, NH2, esters — identification and naming

questions.stem: Which functional group is present in alcohols?
questions.explanation: Alcohols carry the hydroxyl (−OH) group attached to a saturated carbon. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propanol C₃H₇OH. Distinct from phenols where −OH is attached to an aromatic ring. Other groups: −COOH = carboxylic acid; −CHO = aldehyde; −NH₂ = amine; −CO− (between carbons) = ketone; −OR = ether; −COOR = ester.

questions.stem: Acetic acid (vinegar's main component) belongs to which class of organic compounds?
questions.explanation: Acetic acid CH₃COOH — carries the −COOH (carboxyl) group → carboxylic acid. Vinegar is a 4-8% aqueous solution of acetic acid. IUPAC name: ethanoic acid. Carboxylic acids are weak acids (pKa ~4.76 for acetic) — partially dissociate to give H⁺ and acetate ion. Reactions: acid + alcohol → ester + water (Fischer esterification, a classic SSC question).

questions.stem: Formaldehyde (HCHO) — used in biological preservation and resin manufacture — is the simplest:
questions.explanation: Aldehydes have −CHO at the end of a carbon chain. HCHO (formaldehyde / methanal) — simplest aldehyde, only 1 C. Next: CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde / ethanal). Aldehydes give Tollens' (silver mirror) and Fehling's tests positive — distinguishes them from ketones. Formaldehyde is a 37% solution called formalin — used to preserve cadavers, biological specimens, and as a precursor to Bakelite plastic.

questions.stem: Methylamine (CH₃NH₂) belongs to the class of compounds called:
questions.explanation: Amines — derivatives of NH₃ where 1, 2 or 3 hydrogens are replaced by alkyl/aryl groups → primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH), tertiary (R₃N). CH₃NH₂ has just one alkyl on N → primary amine. Amines are basic (lone pair on N can accept H⁺); cause the 'fishy' smell. Examples: aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) — primary aromatic amine, used in dyes; trimethylamine (CH₃)₃N — tertiary, the smell of rotten fish.

questions.stem: The pleasant fruity smell in many ripe fruits and perfumes is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Esters (−COOR) — formed by carboxylic acid + alcohol with H₂SO₄ catalyst (Fischer esterification). Common fruit-aroma esters: ethyl butanoate (pineapple), n-octyl acetate (orange), isoamyl acetate (banana), methyl salicylate (wintergreen). Industrial uses — solvents, perfumes, artificial flavours, plasticisers. Saponification = ester + NaOH → soap + alcohol (basis of soap-making).

questions.stem: Acetone (propan-2-one, CH₃COCH₃) — a common solvent in nail-polish remover — has which functional group?
questions.explanation: Acetone CH₃−CO−CH₃ — the carbonyl (C=O) sits BETWEEN two alkyl groups → ketone. Aldehydes have C=O at the END of the chain (−CHO). Acetone is the simplest ketone; produced industrially from cumene hydroperoxide alongside phenol. A natural product of fat metabolism — elevated in diabetic ketoacidosis (giving breath a 'fruity' smell). Boiling point 56 °C; miscible with water.

questions.stem: Match the functional group with its IUPAC suffix used in nomenclature — which pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: IUPAC suffix for carboxylic acids is '-oic acid' (e.g., ethanoic acid for CH₃COOH), NOT '-ene' (which is the suffix for alkenes / double bond). Other key suffixes: alkanes '-ane', alkenes '-ene', alkynes '-yne', alcohols '-ol', aldehydes '-al', ketones '-one', amines '-amine', esters '-oate', amides '-amide'. Match the suffix carefully — exam papers love this trap.
